| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-64600" by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve, Vulnerabilities.category
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
chsh spawned from user-writable path (RefluXFS reflink-unshare reset primitive) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the RefluXFS exploit precondition step: the advisory notes an unprivileged user runs chsh to reset a target block back to 'unshared' so the race can fire. Flags chsh invoked by a parent binary living in a world/user-writable directory (dropped/compiled exploit) under a non-root account — abnormal versus interactive chsh launched from a login shell. Rationale: The Qualys advisory explicitly calls out chsh as the unprivileged reset step for the reflink 'unshared block' precondition; pairing chsh with a parent binary in /tmp,/dev/shm,/home separates exploit use from a user interactively changing their shell from a login session. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600 • https://gbhackers.com/critical-refluxfs-linux-kernel-flaw/
ATT&CKT1068 T1548
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately changing their login shell via a wrapper script stored in their home directory
  • Configuration-management tooling (Ansible/Salt) staged in /tmp or /var/tmp invoking chsh to set service-account shells
  • Automated provisioning of dev containers that set user shells from a /home build script
  • Security tooling or CTF/lab exploit-testing that intentionally runs chsh
  • Dotfile installers cloned into /home that run chsh during setup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","salt-minion","puppet","cloud-init")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent process command line and hash; confirm whether the parent is a legitimate signed/packaged tool or an unsigned binary dropped in /tmp,/dev/shm,/home, and whether the host is XFS reflink=1 and unpatched for CVE-2026-64600. 2) Contain: isolate the host and suspend the non-root account; capture the parent binary for analysis before it is deleted. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for rapid FICLONE/O_DIRECT file activity by the same PID and for the auth-less root-shell signal (UC3); review /etc/passwd and setuid-root binary contents against a known-good baseline since RefluXFS overwrites leave metadata untouched.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "chsh"
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and AccountName !in~ ("root")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/tmp/","/home/","/run/user/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/chsh" or TargetProcessName =~ "chsh"
| where ActorUsername != "root" and isnotempty(ActorUsername)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/tmp/","/home/","/run/user/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: chsh Launched From User-Writable Directory (RefluXFS reflink-unshare reset)
id: 8b1f2c4a-6d3e-4a19-9f27-2c5a1e0b7d34
description: Detects the chsh binary invoked by a parent process residing in a world- or user-writable directory under a non-root account, matching the RefluXFS (CVE-2026-64600) exploit step that resets an XFS block to unshared state.
references:
  - https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/nine-year-old-refluxfs-linux-flaw-gives.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23
tags:
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.t1548
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '/chsh'
    ParentImage|contains:
      - '/tmp/'
      - '/dev/shm/'
      - '/var/tmp/'
      - '/home/'
      - '/run/user/'
  filter_root:
    User: 'root'
  condition: selection and not filter_root
level: medium
source:(linux.auditd OR linux.syslog) @process.name:chsh -@user.name:root (@process.command_line:*\/tmp\/* OR @process.command_line:*\/dev\/shm\/* OR @process.command_line:*\/home\/*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/chsh$/i
| ParentImageFileName=/\/(tmp|dev\/shm|var\/tmp|home|run\/user)\//i
| NOT UserName=/^root$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, ParentImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.process_name="chsh" (Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_path IN ("/tmp/*","/dev/shm/*","/var/tmp/*","/home/*","/run/user/*")) NOT Endpoint.Processes.user="root" by Endpoint.Processes.dest, Endpoint.Processes.user, Endpoint.Processes.process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process, Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name, Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.process_name="chsh" (Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_path IN ("/tmp/*","/dev/shm/*","/var/tmp/*","/home/*","/run/user/*")) NOT Endpoint.Processes.user="root" by Endpoint.Processes.dest, Endpoint.Processes.user, Endpoint.Processes.process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process, Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name, Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Auth-less root shell without sudo/su/pkexec lineage (RefluXFS post-exploitation) AIInstallation Medium
Detects a root-owned interactive shell whose parent process ran as a non-root user and is NOT a legitimate privilege-transition binary (sudo/su/pkexec/doas/sshd/login). RefluXFS yields root silently — via a stripped root password or a trojaned setuid-root binary — with no sudo record, so an unexplained non-root→root shell transition is the observable outcome the block-layer write itself hides. Rationale: Because the RefluXFS write bypasses the inode and leaves no kernel log or file-modify event (confirmed by Qualys), the earliest reliable signal is the resulting non-root→root shell with no sudo/su/pkexec ancestor; Defender/ASIM expose both child (AccountName/TargetUsername) and initiating-user (InitiatingProcessAccountName/ActorUsername) making the auth-less transition expressible. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/22/refluxfs-a-linux-kernel-local-privilege-escalation-to-root-in-xfs-cve-2026-64600 • https://securityonline.info/refluxfs-cve-2026-64600-xfs-root/
ATT&CKT1068 T1548.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Setuid-root helper wrappers (e.g. custom SUID launchers, some backup agents) that legitimately spawn a root shell without sudo
  • Init/service managers not in the exclusion list (e.g. supervisord, s6, runit) launching root maintenance shells
  • Monitoring/EDR agents shelling out as root from a non-root-launched daemon
  • Interactive consoles from serial/tty getty paths that record a non-root initiating account
  • CI runners executing privileged build steps inside root containers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("/opt/","/usr/lib/") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/tmp/","/home/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: reconstruct the full process tree — identify the initiating non-root user, the parent binary and its path/hash, and whether any sudo/su/pkexec event exists in the same session (absence is the red flag). Confirm the host is XFS reflink=1 and unpatched for CVE-2026-64600. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the root shell, disable the implicated non-root account, and snapshot the disk. 3) Hunt: diff /etc/passwd (look for a stripped/empty root password field) and validate setuid-root binary integrity via package verification (`rpm -Va`) since RefluXFS preserves ownership/perms/timestamps; pivot to the same account's chsh activity (UC2) and any FICLONE/O_DIRECT bursts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","dash","ksh","fish")
| where AccountName =~ "root"
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountName) and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sudo","su","pkexec","doas","sshd","login","runuser","machinectl","systemd","cron","crond","gdm","lightdm","sddm")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/bash","/sh","/zsh","/dash","/ksh","/fish")
| where TargetUsername =~ "root"
| where isnotempty(ActorUsername) and ActorUsername != "root"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("sudo","/su","pkexec","doas","sshd","login","runuser","machinectl"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(bash|sh|zsh|dash|ksh|fish)$/i
| UserName=/^root$/i
| NOT (ParentBaseFileName=/^(sudo|su|pkexec|doas|sshd|login|runuser|machinectl|systemd|crond|cron|gdm|lightdm|sddm)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.process_name IN ("bash","sh","zsh","dash","ksh","fish") Endpoint.Processes.user="root" NOT Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name IN ("sudo","su","pkexec","doas","sshd","login","runuser","machinectl","systemd","init","cron","crond","gdm","lightdm","sddm") by Endpoint.Processes.dest, Endpoint.Processes.user, Endpoint.Processes.process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process, Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.process_name IN ("bash","sh","zsh","dash","ksh","fish") Endpoint.Processes.user="root" NOT Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name IN ("sudo","su","pkexec","doas","sshd","login","runuser","machinectl","systemd","init","cron","crond","gdm","lightdm","sddm") by Endpoint.Processes.dest, Endpoint.Processes.user, Endpoint.Processes.process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process, Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-64600")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-64600")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Shai-Hulud / GhostAction malicious workflow artifact dropped on runner or repo checkout
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network egress from CI/build host to GhostAction secret-exfil infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] CI runner process POSTing secrets to GhostAction exfil host via curl/wget/node · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Network egress from CI/build host to GhostAction secret-exfil infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from self-hosted GitHub Actions runners (or any host) to the GhostAction campaign's exfiltration infrastructure — the 45.139.104.115 / 216.126.225.129 IPs and the bold-dhawan/objective-hopper .plesk.page and carte-avantage.com domains that received 3,325+ stolen Actions secrets via curl POST. Pure IOC match on confirmed campaign infra, so any hit is a near-certain secret-dump in flight. Rationale: Uses the article's pre-extracted GhostAction IPs (45.139.104.115, 216.126.225.129) and domains (bold-dhawan/objective-hopper.plesk.page, carte-avantage.com), all independently confirmed by GitGuardian/BleepingComputer as the campaign's secret-exfil endpoints — hard IOCs, near-zero benign contact. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.gitguardian.com/ghostaction-campaign-3-325-secrets-stolen/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-steal-3-325-secrets-in-ghostaction-github-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/ghostaction-campaign-over-3-000-secrets-stolen-through-malicious-github-workflows
ATT&CKT1567 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or malware sandbox intentionally connecting to the IOC hosts for validation
  • Threat-intel enrichment/beaconing-check tooling that resolves or pings known-bad domains
  • Firewall logging a blocked/denied connection attempt (still worth reviewing, not a true compromise)
  • A future benign tenant reusing the 45-139-104-115.plesk.page shared-hosting range after takedown
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host — confirm whether it is a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner or CI build agent; pull the initiating process and command line. 2) Contain: block the IOC IPs/domains at egress, isolate the runner, and immediately rotate every secret that runner had access to (npm/PyPI/DockerHub/cloud tokens). 3) Hunt: enumerate all repos whose workflows executed on that runner, review recent .github/workflows commits for injected exfil steps, and pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same host.
let iocIPs = dynamic(["45.139.104.115","216.126.225.129"]);
let iocDomains = dynamic(["bold-dhawan.45-139-104-115.plesk.page","objective-hopper.45-139-104-115.plesk.page","carte-avantage.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (iocIPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (iocDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort

union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog

(DnsEvents

 | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud / GhostAction malicious workflow artifact dropped on runner or repo checkout AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the file-write of the Shai-Hulud worm's signature workflow (shai-hulud-workflow.yml) and its bundle.js payload inside a repo/.github/workflows or runner working directory, plus the article's SHA1 acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038. These are the planted supply-chain artifacts that harvest GitHub Actions secrets; the filename + hash are highly specific. Rationale: Keys on the Shai-Hulud worm's confirmed artifact name shai-hulud-workflow.yml (ReversingLabs/Datadog) plus the article's own SHA1 acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038, scoping bundle.js to CI/runner paths to keep it high-fidelity for the supply-chain drop the article warns about. Cross-checked against: • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A researcher cloning a compromised repo into a lab machine for analysis
  • EDR/AV quarantine or backup software creating a copy of the malicious file (write event on a security tool path)
  • A remediation/scanner tool writing the IOC filename as a signature sample
  • A developer intentionally checking in a same-named benign workflow (rare given the exact name)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","veeam.backup.shell.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (git, node, runner agent) and the repo/path; check whether the workflow already executed on this host. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, remove/quarantine the file, and rotate all secrets the affected repo/runner could read (npm publishing tokens first — Shai-Hulud reuses them to publish trojanized packages). 3) Hunt: search the org's repos for the same filename/hash and for recent commits by unfamiliar contributors adding .github/workflows files across many repos in a short window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "shai-hulud-workflow.yml"
   or SHA1 == "acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038"
   or (FileName =~ "bundle.js" and FolderPath has_any (@"\.github\", @"\_work\", @"\actions-runner\", "/.github/", "/_work/"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "shai-hulud-workflow.yml"
   or TargetFileSHA1 =~ "acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038"
   or (TargetFileName =~ "bundle.js" and TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.github\", "/.github/", "/_work/", @"\_work\"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI runner process POSTing secrets to GhostAction exfil host via curl/wget/node AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a process on a self-hosted runner or build host invoking curl/wget/node/powershell with the GhostAction exfil hosts embedded in the command line — the on-runner footprint of the injected workflow step that curl-POSTs the harvested secret context to attacker infrastructure. Combines execution telemetry with confirmed campaign IOCs in the invocation string. Rationale: Matches the GhostAction exfil hosts appearing directly in a process command line — the runner-side signature of the curl POST that GitGuardian documented shipping secrets to these domains; command-line IOC presence is high-fidelity regardless of the interpreter used. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.gitguardian.com/ghostaction-campaign-3-325-secrets-stolen/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-steal-3-325-secrets-in-ghostaction-github-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1059 T1567 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst manually running curl against the IOC host to validate takedown/sinkhole status
  • Threat-intel enrichment or connectivity-check script that references the IOC in its arguments
  • Detection-engineering test/purple-team replay of the GhostAction payload in a lab
  • Backup or copy operation that includes the IOC string in a filename argument
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and parent process; determine if this ran inside a workflow step on a runner vs an interactive analyst session. 2) Contain: kill/isolate the host, block the IOC hosts at egress, and rotate every secret exposed to that workflow run (prioritize npm/PyPI publishing tokens to prevent downstream package poisoning). 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 network hits on the same host, review the triggering workflow's git history for the injected curl step, and check package registries for unexpected publishes using the potentially stolen tokens.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bold-dhawan.45-139-104-115.plesk.page","objective-hopper.45-139-104-115.plesk.page","carte-avantage.com","45.139.104.115","216.126.225.129")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bold-dhawan.45-139-104-115.plesk.page","objective-hopper.45-139-104-115.plesk.page","carte-avantage.com","45.139.104.115","216.126.225.129")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002

| where AccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038") or SHA1 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038") or MD5 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038") or SHA1 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038") or MD5 in~ ("acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["acac5a9854650c4ae2883c4740bf87d34120c038"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NodeBB remote federated-user profile lookup (ActivityPub XSS #1 trigger) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound requests to NodeBB's /user/<name>@<domain> route, which forces the server to webfinger-resolve and fetch a remote ActivityPub actor whose icon.url is rendered unescaped into an og:image <meta> tag (buildMetaTag sink). A victim clicking such a link to an attacker-controlled instance is the delivery vector for the reflected XSS fixed in NodeBB 4.14.0. Surfaces which external handles/domains are being resolved so an analyst can spot lures to attacker.tld / ephemeral tunnel instances. Rationale: Anchored on the exact NodeBB federation route /user/<name>@<domain> from the article's PoC (https://nodebb.local/user/xss@attacker.tld) — the sole inbound signal that forces the server to fetch and render a remote actor's unescaped icon.url. Handles both raw '@' and URL-encoded '%40'. Cross-checked against: • https://community.nodebb.org/topic/19387/nodebb-v4.14.0-federation-regression-fixes-security-fixes-and-more • https://github.com/NodeBB/NodeBB/security/advisories/GHSA-wx69-rvg3-x7fc
ATT&CKT1189 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate federation: real users browsing genuine remote Fediverse/NodeBB/Lemmy actors (e.g. someuser@mastodon.social)
  • Search-engine or link-preview crawlers hitting shared federated profile URLs
  • Fediverse relay/aggregator bots resolving remote handles
  • Admins testing federation against known-good partner instances
  • Users pasting handles copied from other platforms
Suppression filter
| where RemoteHandleDomain !in~ ("mastodon.social","lemmy.world","lemmy.ml")   // extend with your org's known-good federation partners
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract RemoteHandleDomain from the hits; check whether the domain is a known federation partner or a newly-seen/ephemeral host (e.g. *.trycloudflare.com, freshly-registered). Correlate the client IP/user who requested it. 2) Contain: if the target NodeBB is <4.14.0, expedite upgrade (fix commit 4c4bf76 escapes federated data); temporarily disable ActivityPub or block outbound resolution to the suspicious domain at the egress proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'Outbound ActivityPub actor fetch' for the same domain, and review admin session activity for any account whose browser rendered the profile (session hijack via alert(origin) equivalent).
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsUriStem startswith "/user/"
| where CsUriStem contains "@" or CsUriStem contains "%40"
| extend RemoteHandleDomain = extract(@"/user/[^/@]+(?:@|%40)([A-Za-z0-9._-]+)", 1, CsUriStem)
| where isnotempty(RemoteHandleDomain)
| summarize Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Clients = make_set(CIp, 20) by RemoteHandleDomain, CsUriStem, CsHost
| order by FirstSeen desc

NodeBB server outbound ActivityPub/webfinger fetch to ephemeral tunnel or new domain AIExploitation Medium
Detects the NodeBB server making outbound /.well-known/webfinger and /ap/actor ActivityPub discovery requests to attacker-controlled federation instances — the server-side fetch that pulls the malicious actor JSON (icon.url XSS payload) or a rogue signing key. Flags ephemeral Cloudflare tunnel destinations (observed in the research setup) and federation partners never seen before in the baseline window. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete ActivityPub discovery paths (/.well-known/webfinger, /ap/actor/) plus the pre-extracted ephemeral-tunnel IOC (*.trycloudflare.com, the host attacker.tld was fronted by) and a newly-seen-partner anti-join. Server-side outbound fetch is the pivot that distinguishes exploitation from normal browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://community.nodebb.org/topic/19387/nodebb-v4.14.0-federation-regression-fixes-security-fixes-and-more
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate first-time federation with a new but benign remote instance
  • Developers/researchers self-hosting a test Fediverse instance on a Cloudflare tunnel
  • Relay/Lemmy federation resuming after the 4.14.0 upgrade contacting many new hosts at once
  • Link-unfurl or preview services proxied through the same egress path
  • Security scanners probing the org's ActivityPub endpoints
Suppression filter
| where DstHostname !in~ ("mastodon.social","lemmy.world","lemmy.ml")   // known-good federation partners
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source is the NodeBB host and the destination is not a sanctioned federation partner; resolve the domain age/hosting (ephemeral tunnels + <30-day domains are suspicious). 2) Contain: block egress to the destination host and, if the icon.url XSS is unpatched (<4.14.0), disable ActivityPub until upgraded. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 inbound /user/<h>@<domain> requests for the same domain, and check admin/moderator sessions rendered around the fetch time for token/session anomalies indicating a successful stored/reflected XSS.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","nodejs.exe","node")
| where RemoteUrl has "/.well-known/webfinger" or RemoteUrl has "/ap/actor" or RemoteUrl endswith "trycloudflare.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

NodeBB ActivityPub inbox POST carrying HTML-breakout id (Federation Errors stored XSS) AIExploitation Low
Detects unauthenticated POSTs to the NodeBB ActivityPub inbox where the request body's actor/object 'id' contains HTML metacharacters ( "> < img onerror ). Per the article, inbox.js processes signed Update activities and logs failures into the admin Federation Errors view where {./id} is emitted with auto-escaping disabled (identity function), so a crafted id stores XSS that fires when an administrator opens the log. Requires WAF/proxy request-body capture. Rationale: Anchored on the article's second sink: inbox.js handling signed Update activities and the unescaped {./id} in errors.tpl (Benchpress __escape replaced with identity). Matches POST to the /inbox path plus HTML-breakout tokens in the captured body/query. Confidence Low because it depends on WAF body logging. Cross-checked against: • https://community.nodebb.org/topic/19387/nodebb-v4.14.0-federation-regression-fixes-security-fixes-and-more
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1211
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign remote instances whose actor id legitimately contains encoded characters flagged by the naive payload match
  • WAF already normalizing/decoding bodies causing double-encoded false hits
  • Federation debugging tools posting malformed test activities
  • Security scanners fuzzing the ActivityPub inbox
  • Relay software posting large batched activities that trip the substring match
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the request body and confirm the actor/object 'id' actually contains a script/HTML-breakout ( "><img onerror ) rather than benign encoding; note the source instance and signing key. 2) Contain: if NodeBB <4.14.0, do NOT open the admin Federation Errors page from a privileged browser session (it would fire the stored payload); upgrade first, then purge stored federation error entries. 3) Hunt: check whether any admin/global-moderator account viewed the Federation Errors panel after the malicious POST, and review those sessions and admin actions for XSS-driven account or CSRF-style changes.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/inbox"
| where Message has_any ("onerror", "<img", "\">", "%22%3E", "&quot;&gt;") or RequestContext has_any ("onerror", "<img", "\">")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ubuntu snap-confine Flaw Could Give Local Users Root on Default Desktop Installs

The Hacker News
2026-07-22 16 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerability in snap-confine that an unprivileged user can trigger to obtain root access and gain complete control of a target environment. The high-severity flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-8933 (CVSS score: 7.8), impacts default installations of Ubuntu Desktop 24.04, 25.10, and 26.04. The disclosure comes as

CVEsCVE-2026-8933
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Ubuntu hosts exposed to snap-confine LPE CVE-2026-8933 (unpatched snapd) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Malicious udev .rules file written to /run/udev/rules.d by non-root process (CVE-2026-8933) · [LLM] systemd-udevd spawning a shell or interpreter as root (snap-confine CVE-2026-8933 payload execution) · [LLM] snap-confine spawned by an interactive user shell instead of snapd (CVE-2026-8933 trigger) · [LLM] Unprivileged FUSE mount over snap-confine /tmp scratch directory (CVE-2026-8933) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Malicious udev .rules file written to /run/udev/rules.d by non-root process (CVE-2026-8933) AIExploitation High
Hunts the AppArmor-bypass payload of the snap-confine LPE: an unprivileged process dropping a .rules file into the udev rules directory that snap-confine's writable /run/udev path allows. On patch, systemd-udevd reloads and executes the injected commands as root, so a non-root writer of a udev rule is the highest-fidelity artifact of the exploit. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact AppArmor-bypass path (/run/udev/rules.d/*.rules) plus the non-root writer condition; Qualys confirms the exploit drops a malicious udev rule into this allowed path. Legit udev rules are installed by dpkg/root, so a non-root .rules writer is near-unambiguous. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/21/cve-2026-8933-snap-confine-local-privilege-escalation • https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-8933 • https://securityaffairs.com/195833/security/cve-2026-8933-ubuntu-security-flaw-breaks-snap-sandbox-protections.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin manually authoring a udev rule via sudo -e but session logged under original (non-root) username on some agent mappings
  • Configuration-management agents (Ansible/Puppet/Chef) running as a service account rather than root dropping udev rules
  • Third-party hardware driver installers (e.g. GPU, Yubico, printer packages) that write rules to /etc/udev/rules.d under a packaging user
  • Developers testing custom udev rules on a workstation
  • Snap/flatpak tooling writing legitimate device rules during install
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dpkg","apt","unattended-upgrade","systemd-udevd") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","puppet","chef-client"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full file content of the dropped .rules file and the InitiatingProcess lineage; a rule containing RUN+=, PROGRAM= or IMPORT{program} invoking a shell/payload confirms exploit intent. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the writing process tree, remove the malicious rule, and force-reload udev only after verification (udevadm control --reload is what fires the payload). 3) Hunt: check the same host for snap-confine spawned by a user shell, fusermount activity over /tmp/snap*, and any new root processes spawned by systemd-udevd in the surrounding minutes; verify snapd version against the patched 2.76+ubuntuXX builds.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "/run/udev/rules.d" or FolderPath has "/etc/udev/rules.d"
| where FileName endswith ".rules"
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountName) and InitiatingProcessAccountName != "root"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has "/run/udev/rules.d" or TargetFilePath has "/etc/udev/rules.d"
| where TargetFilePath endswith ".rules"
| where isnotempty(ActorUsername) and ActorUsername != "root"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-root Write of udev Rule File (snap-confine CVE-2026-8933)
id: 3f2a6c14-9b7e-4d21-8a55-1c0f9e7b2a44
description: Detects creation or modification of a .rules file under /run/udev/rules.d or /etc/udev/rules.d by a non-root user, the AppArmor-bypass payload of the snap-confine LPE CVE-2026-8933.
references:
  - https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/21/cve-2026-8933-snap-confine-local-privilege-escalation
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ubuntu-snap-confine-flaw-could-give.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23
tags:
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.t1546
  - attack.privilege_escalation
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/run/udev/rules.d/'
      - '/etc/udev/rules.d/'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.rules'
  filter_root:
    User: 'root'
  condition: selection and not filter_root
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*"/run/udev/rules.d"* OR *"/etc/udev/rules.d"*) -@user.name:root
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\/(run|etc)\/udev\/rules\.d\/.+\.rules$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="/run/udev/rules.d/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/udev/rules.d/*") Filesystem.file_name="*.rules" Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="/run/udev/rules.d/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/udev/rules.d/*") Filesystem.file_name="*.rules" Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
systemd-udevd spawning a shell or interpreter as root (snap-confine CVE-2026-8933 payload execution) AIExploitation High
Detects the payoff step of the snap-confine LPE: after the attacker plants a malicious udev rule and triggers a reload, systemd-udevd (running as root) executes the injected command. A udev daemon spawning sh/bash/python or file-permission utilities is the root-code-execution moment of the exploit. Rationale: systemd-udevd legitimately execs device-management helpers (ip, modprobe, hwdb tools) but never an interactive shell or python; the article states the exploit 'forces systemd-udevd to execute arbitrary commands as root', making udevd->shell a direct exploit signature. Datadog left empty: the listed linux.auditd schema exposes no parent-process field, so the parent->child pivot cannot be expressed there. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/21/cve-2026-8933-snap-confine-local-privilege-escalation • https://securityonline.info/snap-confine-cve-2026-8933/
ATT&CKT1068 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A custom, legitimately-installed udev rule using RUN+= to call a helper shell script for hotplug automation
  • Backup/imaging tooling that ships a udev rule invoking a wrapper script
  • Embedded/IoT device provisioning that uses udev RUN rules to run setup shells
  • Hardware vendor rules that call chmod/chown on newly appeared device nodes
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/lib/udev/","/usr/lib/udev/") and FileName in~ ("sh","bash"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine - a reverse shell, chmod 4755, useradd, or write to /etc/passwd/sudoers confirms compromise; benign RUN rules call a fixed wrapper path. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the spawned root process and its descendants, snapshot memory/disk for IR. 3) Hunt: enumerate all /run/udev/rules.d and /etc/udev/rules.d entries for RUN+=/PROGRAM= lines, review preceding snap-confine executions and any /tmp/snap* FUSE mounts, and check for newly created privileged accounts or SUID binaries.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)

snap-confine spawned by an interactive user shell instead of snapd (CVE-2026-8933 trigger) AIExploitation Medium
Detects abnormal invocation of snap-confine directly from a user shell or scripting interpreter. Legitimate snap launches reach snap-confine via snapd/the snap binary; the LPE requires the attacker to drive snap-confine from a controlled user context to win the sandbox-setup race, so a shell as its direct parent is a strong trigger signal. Rationale: Uses the article's named binary /usr/lib/snapd/snap-confine and the fact that post-hardening it runs with the caller's UID; the differentiator is the parent - legit launches go snap/snapd, exploit drives it from a shell. Marked hunting/medium because power users invoking snaps in unusual ways can produce benign hits. Datadog empty: linux.auditd schema has no parent-process field for this pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/21/cve-2026-8933-snap-confine-local-privilege-escalation • https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-8933
ATT&CKT1068 T1548.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or CI job scripting snap application launches from a shell wrapper
  • Debugging snap confinement with gdb/strace attached to snap-confine
  • Automation tools (Ansible shell module) launching snaps non-interactively
  • Custom .desktop launchers or window-manager scripts that exec snap-confine paths directly
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("strace","ltrace") or AccountName in~ ("jenkins","gitlab-runner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the snap-confine command line and the parent shell's recent history; benign use names a real snap, while rapid repeated invocations (race-winning loop) or invocations paired with /tmp FUSE mounts indicate exploitation. 2) Contain: if paired with a udev-rule drop or a root shell, isolate the host and preserve evidence. 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host/user for fusermount over /tmp/snap*, symlink creation in the snap scratch dir, and systemd-udevd child shells; confirm snapd is on a patched 2.76+ubuntu build.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "snap-confine" or FolderPath has "/usr/lib/snapd/snap-confine"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","python3","perl","tmux","screen","gdb")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "snap-confine"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("/bash","/sh","/dash","/zsh","/python3","/perl","/tmux","/screen","/gdb")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unprivileged FUSE mount over snap-confine /tmp scratch directory (CVE-2026-8933) AIExploitation Medium
Detects a non-root user invoking fusermount/mount.fuse against a snap-related /tmp scratch path. The CVE-2026-8933 exploit mounts a malicious FUSE filesystem over the temporary directory snap-confine creates, bypassing mount-namespace isolation so the attacker-controlled directory stays writable during the ownership-transfer race. Rationale: Ties the article's 'mounts a malicious FUSE file system over the temporary scratch directory' to concrete fusermount/mount.fuse execution, scoped by non-root user and a snap-related command line to separate it from generic AppImage/gvfs FUSE usage. Medium fidelity because AppImage launches also use fusermount under /tmp - the 'snap' string is the disambiguator. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/21/cve-2026-8933-snap-confine-local-privilege-escalation • https://securityaffairs.com/195833/security/cve-2026-8933-ubuntu-security-flaw-breaks-snap-sandbox-protections.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AppImage applications launched from a snap-named directory triggering fusermount under /tmp
  • sshfs/gvfs/rclone mounts whose paths coincidentally contain the string 'snap'
  • Developers testing custom FUSE filesystems referencing snap package names
  • Snap desktop integration tooling performing legitimate squashfs/FUSE operations
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/tmp/.mount_" or ProcessCommandLine has ".AppImage")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the fusermount command line for the exact mount target - a FUSE mount landing on snap-confine's /tmp scratch directory (not a squashfs under /snap) is anomalous; check timing against nearby snap-confine invocations. 2) Contain: if correlated with snap-confine spawned by a shell or a udev-rule drop, isolate the host and unmount the rogue FUSE mount after evidence capture. 3) Hunt: look for symlink creation in the scratch dir, 0666 permission changes on snap-owned temp files, and systemd-udevd root shells within the same session; validate snapd patch level.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("fusermount","fusermount3","mount.fuse","mount.fuse3")
| where isnotempty(AccountName) and AccountName != "root"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "snap"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/fusermount","/fusermount3","/mount.fuse","/mount.fuse3")
| where isnotempty(ActorUsername) and ActorUsername != "root"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "snap"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ubuntu hosts exposed to snap-confine LPE CVE-2026-8933 (unpatched snapd) AIReconnaissance High
Exposure hunt surfacing every managed Linux endpoint whose installed snapd/snap-confine is still vulnerable to CVE-2026-8933. Scopes the response perimeter (workstations, dev boxes, admin endpoints) so patching to the fixed 2.76+ubuntu builds can be prioritized before the LPE is weaponized. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id from the article (CVE-2026-8933) against TVM/vuln-scanner telemetry; the article stresses that patched systems can still carry the affected snap-confine variant, so admins must verify installed snapd version rather than release age - this UC operationalizes that guidance. Cross-checked against: • https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-8933 • https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2026/07/21/cve-2026-8933-snap-confine-local-privilege-escalation
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already patched to 2.76+ubuntu24.04.1 / 26.04.3 / 22.04.1 but with stale TVM inventory not yet re-scanned
  • Containers/images reporting a snapd package that is never actually executed
  • Non-desktop server images where snapd is present but snap-confine is unused
  • Endpoints pending reboot after patch where the running version differs from installed
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is below the fixed 2.76+ubuntuXX.YY build for each host's release, and cross-check against the live version (snap version) since TVM inventory can lag. 2) Contain: prioritize patching internet-exposed and multi-user/admin endpoints; where patching is delayed, monitor the four behavioral UCs above as compensating controls. 3) Hunt: for any host that stayed unpatched, retro-hunt DeviceFileEvents/DeviceProcessEvents for the udev-rule drop, FUSE-over-snap mounts, and udevd root shells over the exposure window.

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
