title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental

    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Kratos phishing kit web-asset fingerprint (barr.svg + lg.svg / PTT-SOft path) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Kratos PhaaS credential-exfil POST to next.php / save.php on phishing host · [LLM] Microsoft 365 successful sign-in sourced from Kratos operator IP 41.128.0.142
Kratos PhaaS network/DNS egress to phishing domains and operator IP 41.128.0.142 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts endpoint or perimeter contact with the seized Kratos phishing-as-a-service domains and the Egyptian operator IP 41.128.0.142. Article-specific because it keys on the exact domain set and shared operator IP tied to the fake Microsoft 365 login infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the article's exact seized Kratos domain set plus operator IP 41.128.0.142, both confirmed by ANY.RUN's Kratos write-up which maps them to the fake M365 login infrastructure. IOC-anchored, so FP is essentially limited to sinkhole/researcher traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/german-authorities-dismantle-kratos-phishing-as-a-service-infrastructure • https://www.presseportal.de/blaulicht/pm/7/6318131
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating the phishing URL from a corporate host
  • Threat-intel/sinkhole crawlers hosted in the environment resolving the domains
  • A .de/.es compromised-but-legitimate WordPress site (e.g. crm-technik.de) being visited for benign reasons after cleanup
  • URL-scanning email gateway or Safe Links backend detonation traffic
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("safelinks","urldetonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved or connected, pull the InitiatingProcess (expect a browser) and confirm it was a real user session vs. a scanner. 2) Contain: if a real user reached a fake M365 page, force an Entra ID password reset AND revoke all sessions/refresh tokens (password reset alone is insufficient — Kratos steals session cookies), block the domains/IP at proxy and DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same user for anomalous sign-ins, new inbox rules, and OAuth grants; check other hosts for the same domain/IP contact.

Kratos phishing kit web-asset fingerprint (barr.svg + lg.svg / PTT-SOft path) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Kratos kit's static-asset fingerprint: a browser session requesting both /assets/img/barr.svg and /assets/img/lg.svg (or the /PTT/SOft/ path, or dsa.svg+sid.gif), which ANY.RUN reports as ~90% recall with near-zero FPs for the fake Microsoft 365 login page. Article-specific because these asset paths and their content hashes are unique to the Kratos kit. Rationale: Uses ANY.RUN's V1 fingerprint (barr.svg + lg.svg in one session, ~90% recall), V0 (/PTT/SOft/) and V2 (dsa.svg + sid.gif); the assets' content hashes (barr.svg 949895df..., lg.svg cd231b89..., styles.css c447e75f..., ani.gif 9d1a1a5e...) are the article's SHA256 IOCs, confirming the kit. Requiring the asset pair, not a single generic file, keeps FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://gbhackers.com/kratos-phaas-targets-microsoft-365/
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign site coincidentally serving files named lg.svg and barr.svg in the same 5-minute window (rare; the pair is the discriminator)
  • Safe Links / URL-scanner backend detonating the phishing page
  • Analyst re-detonating the URL during triage
  • Web-archive / cache proxy replaying the captured page
Suppression filter
| where Requests > 1
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the requesting host+user actually rendered the page (both assets present) vs. a scanner; capture the parent domain hosting the assets. 2) Contain: treat as credential theft — force password reset and revoke Entra ID sessions/tokens for the user, block the host domain at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: search Entra sign-ins for that user from new IPs (especially 41.128.0.142), review new inbox forwarding rules and OAuth consents, and sweep other hosts for the same asset fingerprint.

Kratos PhaaS credential-exfil POST to next.php / save.php on phishing host AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-harvesting HTTP POST from a victim browser to the Kratos exfil endpoints (/next.php, /nex.php, /n3xt.php, /save.php, /SOft/mini.php) on a known Kratos domain or the operator IP. Article-specific because it pairs the kit's exact exfil filenames with the seized infrastructure, indicating credentials were actually submitted. Rationale: Uses ANY.RUN's documented Kratos exfil endpoints (next.php / nex.php / n3xt.php / save.php / SOft/mini.php with POST params di,pr) anchored to the article's seized domains and operator IP 41.128.0.142, so a match means credentials were actually POSTed — a confirmed-victim signal, not just a page view. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/kratos-phaas-attacking-microsoft-365-users/
ATT&CKT1056.003 T1539
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate app on a compromised .de/.es host using next.php/save.php naming (mitigated by requiring the Kratos domain/IP)
  • Researcher submitting decoy credentials during triage
  • Automated form-fuzzing / DAST scanner hitting the phishing host
  • Safe Links backend detonation submitting a synthetic credential
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the POST originated from a real user browser session and identify the account; treat any TRUE match as a credential-compromise event. 2) Contain: immediately reset the user's Entra ID password and revoke all sessions and refresh tokens (Kratos steals cookies/tokens — reset alone is insufficient), enforce MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: review SigninLogs for that account from 41.128.0.142 and other new IPs, check for newly created inbox rules, mail-forwarding, OAuth app consents, and outbound BEC-themed mail to the user's contacts.

Inbound email with URL to Kratos phishing domain clicked via Safe Links AIDelivery High
Correlates delivered inbound email carrying a URL to a Kratos phishing domain with a subsequent Safe Links click by the recipient. Article-specific because it filters on the exact seized Kratos domain set rather than generic phishing heuristics, and flags the click-through that turns delivery into likely compromise. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact seized Kratos domains in delivered inbound email URLs, then joins Safe Links click telemetry to prioritise recipients who actually clicked — high fidelity because the domain set is the IOC and the click makes credential submission likely. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/german-authorities-dismantle-kratos-phishing-as-a-service-infrastructure
ATT&CKT1566.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Kratos domain that was a compromised-but-legitimate site (e.g. crm-technik.de) also sending benign mail before compromise
  • Internal phishing-simulation campaign reusing a since-seized domain
  • Threat-intel newsletter or IR report email quoting the domain as text (URL present but benign context)
  • Analyst forwarding the phishing sample internally for review
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation in ("Inbox","External")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the message was Delivered (not Blocked/Junked) and whether UrlClickEvents shows a click; prioritise ClickedThrough recipients. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide (ZAP), reset password + revoke sessions/tokens for any recipient who clicked, and block the sender + domains. 3) Hunt: enumerate all recipients of the same NetworkMessageId/cluster, check clicked users' sign-ins from 41.128.0.142, and review for new inbox rules or OAuth grants.

Microsoft 365 successful sign-in sourced from Kratos operator IP 41.128.0.142 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Alerts on any successful Entra ID / M365 sign-in whose source IP is the Kratos operator IP 41.128.0.142, indicating an operator replaying stolen credentials or session tokens for account takeover. Article-specific because it keys on the single operator IP tied to the seized Kratos backend. Rationale: 41.128.0.142 is the Kratos operator IP (Egypt) confirmed by ANY.RUN; any successful M365 sign-in from it is near-certain account takeover, so it is a clean single-IOC alerting rule with essentially zero legitimate FP. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/kratos-phaas-account-takeover/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/kratos-phaas-attacking-microsoft-365-users/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A traveler or VPN egress genuinely using 41.128.0.142 (unlikely — it is dedicated operator infrastructure)
  • Threat-intel enrichment or a red-team exercise deliberately authenticating from that IP
  • Shared NAT if the operator IP were ever reassigned by the hosting provider after seizure
  • Security tooling health-check logins pinned to that address (rare)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the sign-in succeeded (ErrorCode/ResultType 0) and capture the account, app, and conditional-access outcome. 2) Contain: disable the account or force sign-out, reset password AND revoke all refresh/session tokens, require MFA re-registration; block 41.128.0.142 in Conditional Access. 3) Hunt: enumerate all accounts that authenticated from this IP, review each for new inbox rules, mail forwarding, OAuth consents, mass mailbox reads, and outbound BEC mail to contacts.
AADSignInEventsBeta | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where IPAddress == "41.128.0.142" | where ErrorCode == 0 | project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, Application, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, RiskLevelDuringSignIn | order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where IPAddress == "41.128.0.142" | where ResultType == 0 | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState | order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

SecurityEvent

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c") or SHA1 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c") or MD5 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c") or SHA1 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c") or MD5 in~ ("cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["cd231b895bbcd7154b81df1e065bf02f1ec667b920c8b6d23308cd509833b5ea", "949895df17148c5ea29f190d2619a14b3ec648425b9cc3c5a1423553c16f3898", "9d1a1a5e3b5e5de8a6c76ded7a01fa01709d426232b0048c9ee6ba0c5c1b8b42", "c447e75f1029ed7a5882add16bcd13ad44be3bd47c93c830ff39185e23d25ebb", "a3c298ccf2456989ceb080e661b01c3b00445902ae7bb3e58dad4d846334ff9c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gitea vulnerable PR-update API route access (CVE-2026-58443 public-only token bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP POST requests to Gitea's pull-request update endpoint POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/update, the exact route CVE-2026-58443 abuses so a public-only,write:repository token pushes public base commits into a PRIVATE head branch. Article-specific because the route path, method, and behaviour are the vulnerability signature; correlate the captured source IP / authenticated principal against token scope in Gitea's own admin/audit view to confirm exploitation. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable route from the advisory (POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/update) plus HTTP method — the concrete CVE-2026-58443 signature. Defender/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: none of those telemetry sets ship Gitea reverse-proxy request paths+methods; token-scope-vs-target-repo correlation must be finished in Gitea's own audit log. Corroborated fixed version (1.27.0) and route via GitLab advisory and multiple vendor write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xxjv-752h-3vp2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58443/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gitea-vulnerability/ • https://securityonline.info/gitea-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate maintainers clicking the Gitea 'Update branch' button (calls the same API route)
  • CI/CD service accounts programmatically syncing PR branches with the base branch
  • Automated merge/rebase bots (e.g. renovate/dependabot-style) that update PRs
  • Repository owners updating their own private-repo PRs via a fully-scoped token
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, pull the source IP and authenticated principal from the Gitea admin panel; in Gitea, check whether the token used carried the public-only scope and whether the PR's HEAD repository is PRIVATE while the base (route) repo is public — that combination is the exploit, a same-owner fully-scoped update is benign. 2) Contain: revoke and rotate the offending token, and upgrade Gitea to 1.27.0 (patch #38406); temporarily restrict PR-update to authenticated maintainers if patching is delayed. 3) Hunt: enumerate Actions workflow runs in the affected private repo around the event time (the malicious push can trigger private CI), review git push events into private head branches attributable to that token, and check for secrets exfil in those workflow logs.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)/api/v1/repos/[^/]+/[^/]+/pulls/[0-9]+/update"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Gitea instance exposed to CVE-2026-58443 (version <= 1.26.4) AIExploitation High
Surfaces managed hosts running a Gitea build vulnerable to CVE-2026-58443 (all releases up to and including 1.26.4; fixed in 1.27.0) so exposure can be remediated before the public-token-to-private-repo bypass is exploited. Article-specific via the exact CVE identifier and affected product. Rationale: Keys on the concrete CVE-2026-58443 identifier and the Gitea product name; affected-range (<=1.26.4) and fix (1.27.0) confirmed against the GitLab advisory mirror and multiple vendor write-ups. Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty as vuln-state exposure is not carried in FDR/CloudTrail/Datadog log telemetry here. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/code.gitea.io/gitea/CVE-2026-58443/ • https://blog.gitea.com/release-of-1.27.0/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/gitea-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched to 1.27.0 but scanner catalog not yet refreshed (stale finding)
  • Air-gapped/internal-only Gitea with no untrusted token issuance (real but low-risk exposure)
  • Custom/forked Gitea build whose version banner mis-maps to the CVE
  • Container image tag pinned <=1.26.4 in a non-production sandbox
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is truly <= 1.26.4 and that the instance issues API tokens to users beyond trusted admins (public-only tokens are the attack precondition). 2) Contain: schedule/apply the upgrade to Gitea 1.27.0 (patch #38406); until patched, audit and where possible revoke public-only,write:repository tokens and restrict PR-update on public base repos. 3) Hunt: pivot to the CVE-2026-58443 web-route detection for this host to see if the vulnerable endpoint was already exercised, and review recent private-repo Actions workflow triggers.

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-58443")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-58443")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
